description: Feeling and its cultures. Love gets the deepest branch because so many other ideas run through it: attachment, friendship, family, loss, and forgiveness.

concepts.title: Emotion
concepts.summary: Bodies share broad emotional capacities, but cultures teach us what to call a feeling, when to show it, and what it says about a person. Even pride and shame sit in different places on different maps.

concepts.title: Love
concepts.summary: Attention that stays. Cultures give it different forms, such as duty, romance, hospitality, and devotion, but the shape is recognizable: someone else's wellbeing becomes part of yours.

concepts.title: Attachment
concepts.summary: The bond that forms between a child and whoever reliably comforts them, and that echoes through later relationships. A secure early base seems to make it easier to explore, and to trust.

concepts.title: Oxytocin
concepts.summary: A hormone released during birth, nursing, touch, and closeness. It's often called the love chemical, which oversimplifies a system that shapes trust and bonding together with many other signals.

concepts.title: Friendship
concepts.summary: Chosen closeness, without the claims of blood or bargain. Friends witness who you're becoming, and few things predict a long, healthy life as reliably as having a few.

concepts.title: Family
concepts.summary: The people you're bound to before you've chosen anything. It's where language, food, and the first idea of love are learned, and where they're most often unlearned, too.

concepts.title: Forgiveness
concepts.summary: Letting go of the claim on someone for what they did. It isn't excusing it or forgetting; it's deciding the hurt no longer gets to run the story, which often helps the forgiver most.

concepts.title: Unconditional Love
concepts.summary: Love that asks nothing back: the old Greek word for it was agape. Many traditions treat it as the highest kind, and nearly all agree it is easier to admire than to practice.

concepts.title: Loneliness
concepts.summary: The ache of wanting more connection than you have. It's not the same as being alone, and it is a genuine signal, like hunger, that people are built to live among others.

concepts.title: Grief
concepts.summary: What love turns into when the person it was for is gone. It comes in waves, has no schedule, and mostly eases not by ending but by making room around it.

concepts.title: Joy
concepts.summary: A brightness that arrives without asking what it's for. It's often found in ordinary moments, and is easier to notice when you're not chasing it.

concepts.title: Laughter
concepts.summary: An old, social sound that predates language. We laugh far more with others than alone, and it works mostly as a signal: this is safe, we're together.

concepts.title: Gratitude
concepts.summary: Noticing what you were given, by people or by luck. Practiced regularly it tends to shift attention from what's missing to what's here, and it strengthens the ties it points at.

concepts.title: Anger
concepts.summary: The feeling that a line has been crossed. It's information about what someone cares about, and it does the most good when it's understood before it's acted on.

concepts.title: Empathy
concepts.summary: Feeling something of what another person feels, or at least understanding it from the inside. It's what makes care possible, and it's tiring enough that we need to choose where to spend it.

concepts.title: Fear
concepts.summary: An old alarm with many new triggers. Fear points at what might be lost, and each culture decides what's worth fearing and who is allowed to be afraid.

concepts.title: Courage
concepts.summary: Acting well while afraid, not without fear. It's a decision that something matters more than the risk, and it's usually much smaller and quieter than the stories make it seem.

concepts.title: Anxiety
concepts.summary: Fear about what hasn't happened. It has a purpose, to prepare you, but when it can't find a specific danger it loops, and much of coping is learning to tell the two apart.

concepts.title: Shame
concepts.summary: The feeling of being seen falling short. It's deeply social: the same act can bring shame in one place and none in another. Useful in small doses, corrosive when it becomes an identity.

concepts.title: Guilt
concepts.summary: Shame's more useful cousin: not I am bad but I did something wrong. It points toward repair, and it fades when the repair is made or the lesson is learned.

concepts.title: Hope
concepts.summary: A stubborn bet on the shape of tomorrow. It doesn't need evidence to begin, only enough openness to move toward something not yet true.
